https://www.timesfreepress.com/news/2026.text: Prague’s rare 70 mm IMAX draws thousands of Europeans for Nolan’s 'The Odyssey' PRAGUE (AP) — With Christopher Nolan’s highly anticipated “The Odyssey” recording impressive sales around the globe, thousands of Europeans have used it as a new and unexpected reason to visit Prague. The Czech capital has a movie theater that's among the few dozen in the world equipped with the coveted 70 mm IMAX screen to watch the first feature made entirely with IMAX film cameras. “It completely changed my experience about the movie," said Nicolas Walak from Poland, who also saw the movie before on a normal screen before viewing it in Prague. "Everything was great. It was a great movie.” Czech cinema adapts to meet demand for rare IMAX format There are only 41 70 mm IMAX screens worldwide, with most in North America. Montpellier in France and the Belgian capital, Brussels, are the only other two in the European Union countries. Britain has another three. To meet massive demand, the Czech branch of the Cinema City offers four to five screenings a day, one starting after midnight, and the majority are sold out. Film fans from about 15 European countries, from Scandinavia to Spain, have been coming to watch “The Odyssey” in Prague, Cinema City said. Their number reached 22,000 by Monday, it said. The 70 mm IMAX film presentation is Nolan's preferred format. The Oscar-winning filmmaker calls it the “best possible experience.” Moviegoers travel up to three days to Prague Daniel Jung drove with his two teenage sons, Felix and Leo, for three days from Norway through Denmark and Germany "just to see this movie. Tomorrow, we’re going back.” Leo was in touch with Cinema City by email half a year before the July 16 premiere and followed the cinema operator on Instagram. He managed to book the tickets immediately after they became available. “We were in the 11th row, right in the middle. We had the very best seats,” Leo said, calling the effort “absolutely worth it.” “It’s just so big. We come from Norway, the screens we have are much smaller,” he said. “Now, we watched it in this huge format. I will always remember this experience.” Felix said they had a good time on the way, visiting some places in Germany, but it would be worth it even if they just drove straight there. Few IMAX left because of costs and other challenges Due to the cost and other challenges, productions made using large format film are rare. The IMAX cameras are heavy and new versions with reduced noise had to be developed to be usable for making “The Odyssey.” The film print sent to theaters is so big — weighing some 300 kilograms (661 pounds) and 18 kilometers (11 miles) long — that it has to be delivered to theaters in parts. The movie and the projector have to be in a climatized room and the projectionists need to be approved by IMAX for the job. As movie theaters around the globe were acquiring digital IMAX equipment around 2008, the Cinema City decided not to get rid of the original analog projector in Prague. It was placed in a corner for three years until 2012 to screen Nolan’s “The Dark Knight Rises.” It was used to show several others, including Nolan's “Interstellar” in 2014 and “Oppenheimer” three years ago. “We’re really grateful to him for that,” projectionist Tomáš Vyšinský said about his predecessor who saved the equipment. https://hungarytoday.hu/budapest-hotel-r.text: Budapest Hotel Rates Overtake Those in Vienna Budapest’s hotel market emerged as a regional leader in July across several key performance indicators, with the Hungarian capital’s hotels recording a net average daily room rate of €140.20, surpassing Vienna. According to data comparing Budapest, Vienna, Prague, Bratislava, and Warsaw, hotels in the Hungarian capital recorded an occupancy rate of 80.6%, enough for third place. Budapest ranked first, however, in terms of net average room rate, as well as in one of the hotel industry’s key profitability indicators, revenue per available room (RevPAR), which reached €113. Budapest also performed strongly across multiple hotel segments. Compared with Vienna and Prague, Budapest ranked first in net RevPAR in the Luxury & Upper Upscale, Upscale, and Midscale & Economy categories alike, Mfor writes, citing the July industry analysis by the Association of Hungarian Hotels and Restaurants. In other words, Budapest outperformed its two main regional competitors not only in the upper-end hotel segment, but also among mid-range and more affordable properties. Budapest. Photo: Pexels Budapest’s ranking also improved significantly in a broader European comparison. Among the 35 European destinations examined, the city ranked 13th in occupancy at 80.6%, 17th in net average room rate at €140.20, and 16th in RevPAR. This marks a significant improvement from previous years when the Hungarian capital often ranked around 30th, the outlet reports, citing the hotel association’s analysis. Budapest’s strong July performance was largely driven by the Formula 1 race, which this year brought a surge in international visitors and higher room rates in July rather than August, as well as several major international concerts, including performances by Pitbull and Ricky Martin. Strong demand for Budapest was already evident from July’s airport figures, with Liszt Ferenc International Airport handling 2.1 million passengers, up 16% from a year earlier. Budapest hotels benefited from the surge, with total revenue rising 19%. The strong performance was largely driven by Formula 1. More than 310,000 fans attended the Hungarian Grand Prix over four days, setting a new attendance record at the Hungaroring . Hotel rates in Budapest typically rise during the race weekend, particularly at upscale and centrally located properties. National tourism data, however, paints a much more subdued picture . According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), the number of visitors fell 0.4% in July, while the number of overnight stays increased by just 0.3% year over year. The number of foreign visitors declined 1.9%, but the number of nights they spent in Hungary rose by the same percentage, meaning fewer foreign tourists arrived but stayed for longer on average. Many property owners deliberately test the market with extremely high prices. https://www.latintimes.com/brazils-spy-a.text: The Briefing: Brazil's Abin spy agency formally told a French-German EU delegation in Brasília on September 9–11 that both the United States and Russia are actively interfering in the country's presidential election, according to sources and documents reviewed by Reuters. Abin elevated the risk of U.S. pressure on the election to a "critical level" in a confidential report sent in late August to the presidential palace, the Ministry of Justice, and Brazil's Supreme Electoral Court — weeks before European officials arrived for the briefing. Cyberattacks against Brazil nearly doubled year-over-year, with a concentrated surge in hacks and phishing attempts targeting the presidential office that a senior Brazilian cyber official described as clearly "election-related." Three days before Brazilians cast ballots in one of the hemisphere's most closely watched elections, their country's own spy agency has quietly transformed a domestic political feud into a transatlantic intelligence exchange — one with implications for democracies on both sides of the Atlantic and beyond.Brazil's federal intelligence agency, Abin, briefed a joint French-German European Union delegation in Brasília from September 9 to 11, formally confirming active interference in the country's presidential race by both the United States and Russia, according to sources and documents reviewed by Reuters. A written report compiled by a meeting attendee states that Abin officials "confirmed the existence of interference from the United States as well as Russia." The agency described the American operations as ranging "from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged," while offering no specifics on the Russian activities.A European Delegation With Two MissionsThe official purpose of the French-German visit was to assess how Brazil is putting into practice the European Union's Digital Services Act — Brussels' flagship regulation requiring online platforms to more aggressively police harmful and illegal content. Washington has been openly critical of that law, arguing it disproportionately burdens American technology companies.A second, less publicized objective, however, was embedded in the same trip. A document reviewed by Reuters reveals the delegation's visit also aimed at "preparing coordinated responses ahead of the 2026 elections" — meaning the Europeans arrived in Brazil not just as digital regulators, but as intelligence partners mapping shared vulnerabilities in real time.The French contingent came from Viginum, the government body dedicated to detecting foreign digital disinformation campaigns, along with representatives from Arcom, France's media and communications regulatory authority. Germany sent officials from its Federal Network Agency, which regulates telecommunications, energy, rail and postal services. Both Arcom and Viginum confirmed the participation of their representatives in the Brasília meeting. Germany's Federal Network Agency separately noted that possible U.S. meddling in German elections was not a topic discussed at the meeting.Why Paris Is Watching Brasília So CloselyFrench officials have been speaking with unusual candor about what Sunday's Brazilian vote means for their own country. Privately, they described Brazil's October contest to Reuters as an early warning indicator for France's presidential election next year — a striking admission that a race taking place thousands of kilometers away is being studied by European governments as a dress rehearsal for what could come closer to home.That assessment is grounded in a visible pattern: the Trump administration has openly backed right-wing candidates across Europe and Latin America in recent months. In France, far-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads presidential polls. In Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany party finished first in elections in two states last month, officials have been publicly critical of Washington's endorsement of the AfD. Across the Atlantic, the United States extended a bailout potentially worth $40 billion to Argentine President Javier Milei ahead of difficult midterm elections, while U.S. Vice President JD Vance traveled to Hungary to campaign alongside Viktor Orbán.The Pressure Campaign Lula Has Made PersonalThe accusations leveled by Abin are inseparable from the broader deterioration of U.S.-Brazil relations under the current administrations. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking his fourth term in office, has publicly accused the Trump administration of attempting to tilt the race toward his opponent. Lula has pointed to two actions he frames as overt political interference: the announcement of 50 percent tariffs on all Brazilian goods, unveiled July 9, 2025 and set to take effect August 1, 2025, which Trump linked explicitly to Brazil's prosecution of former President Jair Bolsonaro; and the revocation of the Brazilian ambassador's visa in Washington in August 2026, a move the U.S. tied to Brazil's refusal to grant approval for Trump's nominee to be ambassador in Brasília.At the center of that dispute is former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison after a Brazilian Supreme Court panel convicted him of leading a criminal organization and organizing a coup attempt following his defeat in the 2022 election. Bolsonaro has been incarcerated since November 2025, when he was arrested after allegedly cutting through his ankle monitoring bracelet in what the court viewed as a bid to flee the country.His eldest son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, is now carrying that political inheritance into the presidential race. On October 4, he will face Lula in a first-round contest that analysts describe as statistically too close to call, with both leading candidates carrying rejection rates close to 50 percent. If neither secures an outright majority of valid votes, a runoff follows on October 25.Before the European delegation landed in Brasília, Abin had already begun escalating its internal warnings. The agency sent a confidential report to the presidential palace, the Ministry of Justice, and Brazil's Supreme Electoral Court in late August, raising the threat of U.S. pressure on the election to what it labeled a "critical level." The report, first disclosed publicly on September 19 by Folha de S.Paulo and subsequently confirmed by TV Brasil, framed the Trump administration's actions as part of a deliberate strategy to reassert American hegemony in Latin America by curbing the influence of rival powers, particularly China.Brazil Builds Its Cyber Shield Before the VoteThe Brazilian Army ran the eighth edition of its Guardião Cibernético cybersecurity drill from September 21 to 25, drawing more than 1,300 participants, approximately 300 organizations, and representatives from 14 countries across Brasília and six other state capitals — São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Curitiba, Recife, Manaus, and Belém. Described by its organizers as one of the most comprehensive cybersecurity training exercises in the Southern Hemisphere, the drill simulated coordinated digital strikes against critical infrastructure across energy, telecommunications, and financial sectors.The exercise ran the same week the Abin "critical level" report became public, and concluded five days before the Reuters reporting on the European intelligence briefings appeared on September 30. A senior Brazilian cyber official told Reuters that digital attacks on Brazil had nearly doubled year-over-year, with a particular spike in hacks and phishing attempts aimed at the presidential office — activity the official characterized as clearly tied to the electoral calendar.A Pattern That Is Harder to Deny Than to DocumentBoth the U.S. State Department and Russia's embassy in Brasília declined to comment on the Abin briefings. Washington has previously denied seeking to influence Brazilian elections; Moscow has similarly denied election meddling in other countries.What the Abin briefing makes difficult to dismiss is the structural shift it represents. Countries that believe they are targets of foreign political interference are no longer handling that pressure in isolation. They are sharing intelligence across borders, treating each other's election cycles as real-time intelligence inputs, and building the architecture of a counter-network at the same pace that influence operations evolve.With voting beginning in under 72 hours, the question is no longer whether foreign interference will be alleged. The question is whether the evidence gathered by one of the world's most populous democracies — and quietly shared with its European partners — will ultimately matter to anyone who can act on it.

https://www.interviewmagazine.com/music/.text: Art Music Fashion Culture Film Shop Masthead Contact Us CATHARSIS Bassvictim on Growing Up and Getting Sober By Patrick McGraw November 6, 2026 Bassvictim, photographed by Jacob Ortega. For every emotional crisis I’ve been through in the past year, Bassvictim has been the soundtrack. I’ve never heard anyone accurately describe what makes their sound so compelling, but after experiencing the catharsis of it, nothing else seems to suffice. Their intensity can at times be such that, while driving around L.A. listening to them with a friend earlier this year, they suggested that maybe it was the music itself that was causing my crises. The duo, Maria Manow and Ike Clateman, has just released a new album, Peace + War . Recorded in Vietnam this past spring, it is considerably cleaner than their previous work. Though it maintains the at times transcendent honesty, they chose to restrict themselves to using only electronic instruments, as opposed to the live instrumentation they used on last year’s breakout album Forever . It’s the latest in what has been an almost blindingly productive period for the band, with Peace + War making a total of two albums and three EPs they’ve released in just the past couple of years alone. We met at Clateman’s brother’s apartment the night after their Halloween show at Knockdown Center in New York. Sequestered in a side room, they sat across from me on a Freudian divan and spoke for hours about getting violently ill, why they don’t like their new album, and sobriety, while a group of friends made dinner outside. We never did land on a simple definition of their sound. Like almost everything else on earth that is good, it is beyond words. SUNDAY 7:30 PM NOVEMBER 1, 2026 NYC ——— PATRICK MCGRAW: The show last night felt different from the last time I saw you play in March. MARIA MANOW: In what sense? MCGRAW: It was loose in L.A., we were all dancing on stage. But last night was tighter, more professional. MANOW: I think the main thing that changed is my sobriety. CLATEMAN: We also now have a stage designer, and a 12-person crew traveling with us. Before, the Bassvictim shows were an idea. It was portable and we could carry it in our pocket and take it wherever we played and adapt to whatever’s there. MANOW: Bassvictim has become all of these people, they’re all part of this well-oiled machine. Without them we wouldn’t be able to make it right now. MCGRAW: Ike, you were so much more active last night. CLATEMAN: Because I wasn’t being thrown into uncertain situations every night. I had all this time and space to reconfigure my relationship to being on stage. MANOW: It’s a lot easier when the weight of so many components are lifted off your shoulders, you can focus on giving a good performance. I definitely think sobriety helped. Before, I wasn’t thinking of what I was doing. Now, I’m painfully aware of everything around me. It was really hard at the beginning of the tour to get into this professional mode, but once I got out of my head, it was easier. I move a lot more, but I’m really aware of everything and sometimes I get paranoid that people still think that I’m a bit of a mess. Part of the reason why I move so much is because then I feel like people won’t be thinking that I– MCGRAW: You’re proving them wrong. MANOW: Yeah, I’m proving them wrong and they’re like, “Oh, this is the real Maria and she can be sober.” CLATEMAN: I’ve always felt like vices are their own practice. You have to do a lot of them to enjoy any of them. To enjoy a cigarette, you kind of have to be drunk. Once I’m sober, I can’t really enjoy any vices. MCGRAW: You’ve been sober on this tour though, more or less? CLATEMAN: Yeah. MANOW: A sober tour. MCGRAW: You guys had a reputation for the shows being druggy and fucked up, and this is very much not that. CLATEMAN: That was an early days vibe. A band is this creature that emerges from a cesspool and then, once it’s out, it washes the mud off and learns to walk and it emerges out of the trees and then it has to put clothes on. All of this is just part of the trajectory of a band moving from playing in the clubs to being in the studio. It makes sense that as the thing gets bigger, there’s more work to do so you just treat it with more care. MANOW: I’m glad it’s going the way it is. It’s like growing as a child, but I do miss certain elements from the past shows. It was nice to be a part of a greater thing. Now, it’s just us versus them. CLATEMAN: Before the show was the reward. We would make music and then we would get to hear it all loud on these sound systems, and that was so exciting. It was always a surprise if people were really hyped because we didn’t have fans yet. So if a show was really good, it was purely because of our energy and the music we had just made brought this place to life. But now, it’s like we already know they’re going to be excited. MANOW: In some ways the previous opinions felt more honest. CLATEMAN: That is just the thing you can never get back as a band. It’s like a catch-22. You work so hard in these shitty clubs trying to get bigger, and then you get bigger and you try to get back to the shitty clubs. The tours were so rough back then. MANOW: They were really intense. MCGRAW: Did you bring that newfound professionalism to Peace + War ? MANOW: The new album? MCGRAW: The new album. MANOW: I don’t really like it. MCGRAW: Really? CLATEMAN: Neither of us like it as much as Forever , but I’m really curious to see what people think of it. MCGRAW: It is different. It’s very well produced. There’s a certain primal element to Forever that I feel is not as much on the new album, even though it’s really good. MANOW: I agree. We both agree. I can’t listen to that album. CLATEMAN: But it’s weird because we actually downgraded the studio. I just brought a little home studio setup to a bedroom in Vietnam. And on Forever , there was co-production and stuff. Peace + War was just all me on the production side. It was almost back to the old days, but somehow it did come out almost more polished and poppy. MCGRAW: Was that a choice? CLATEMAN: It wasn’t a choice so much as it’s just, like, you don’t want to repeat yourself. MANOW: At least we don’t want to. CLATEMAN: I like to be surprised. So I made the choice to cut myself off from access to all the acoustic instruments and pianos, and go back to just working with my laptop to see what I would do now that we’ve made these two albums with full-on instrument studios. I wanted to strip it back and see what would come out. MANOW: It’s interesting how the space affects the sound. Forever was done in Norway. It was cold and got dark really early. There were so many instruments that we were jamming with. So that sound naturally became the way it did because we recorded there. If we did Peace + War in Norway, it would have sounded more similar. CLATEMAN: That was how I felt too. And that’s why I didn’t want to go back, because I could just see the process being identical and I like the idea of giving yourself obstructions. MANOW: A lot of Forever stuff is based on real instruments, and this is purely digital. I was also ill in Vietnam and getting quite fucked up. I cared less. I had a lot of anger there. Something happened after we made Forever . I was in L.A. and started feeling a lot more unholy or something. I started feeling negative emotions, but in this more aggressive way. So all of these songs sound more aggressive. I was really ill in Vietnam, I lost so much weight. It’s insane. I look at my pictures and it’s like I hardly recognize myself. CLATEMAN: Your skin was green. MANOW: To cope with the illness, I was getting fucked up because I was in so much pain. But then, getting fucked up made it worse. And on top of that, we had our friends filming us. We were in a country that’s super wet and sweaty. CLATEMAN: 100 degree heat. MANOW: 100 degree heat or cold inside because of the AC. I hate those environments and we didn’t have any tools. So making this album just wasn’t a vibe. In Norway, it was such a vibe that we were in this beautiful cozy pod, and then we would come outside of the cozy pod and it would be super crispy. CLATEMAN: For me, it was a vibe. MANOW: For me, it wasn’t. CLATEMAN: We had quite different experiences in Vietnam. For me, it was a perfect pod environment, just this simple setup and lots of beds and TVs and lights and isolation. No one to talk to and no one to see. That’s why the album is so long because I was working constantly. MANOW: Ike was thriving there. CLATEMAN: That did affect the album’s sound. With Forever, there was a glue between everything. The environment and the music, me and Maria, it’s really stuck together. With this album, it feels disconnected in different ways. But I think that’s interesting. MCGRAW: It’s not necessarily a bad thing. CLATEMAN: I think of this as our White Album . It’s a time where we were really prolific, but not super connected and our desires for the project were mysterious to each other. MANOW: I also feel that in some ways I was out of melodies. I know that that’s not true because you’re always going to find new ones, but there were just so many good melodies on Forever. I t was like I came up with every single good melody and every single good lyric and there was nothing else. CLATEMAN: It’s a cool way to think about the album. I think it’s kind of apocalyptic. Like, imagine a world where there are no more melodies left. It’s the end of melodies. MANOW: Part of the reason there are less melodies or hard-hitting lyrics is because I just wasn’t inspired. Forever was so inspired by my breakup. But in the months prior to going to Vietnam, I was just relaxing in L.A. and Poland. So a lot of the songs were more abstract, going back to anger that I felt from the past or health related things because that was going on. “Happysad” is the way I feel about the world now that we have become bigger. Without that intense breakup, I went back to the mindset I had during Basspunk 1 and Basspunk 2 where it was harder to channel consistent inspiration. MCGRAW: I can’t think of any other music that hits you on this guttural level right now. I’m trying to think of what words I would use to describe it, visceral— CLATEMAN: I feel like you experience everything viscerally all the time. MANOW: I experience everything. CLATEMAN: You’re saying you didn’t have the breakup, but the inspirations for Peace + War were just as visceral. MANOW: It was just as visceral. CLATEMAN: Maybe more. MANOW: I think what makes me feel like it’s not as good is that when someone asks me what’s my favorite song, I can’t pick a favorite song. CLATEMAN: I like it as a whole. MANOW: I like it as a whole thing. In previous albums, I liked every single song, but I could pick favorites. CLATEMAN: Yeah, when people are like, “Can I hear a song from the album?” I never know which one. MANOW: I never know which one. CLATEMAN: I’m always looking through every single one of them, and I’m like, “No, but that one’s too, but this one is—” MANOW: Too this, too that. CLATEMAN: “Is too—” MANOW: T oo something. CLATEMAN: “But that one is too—” MCGRAW: “White Flag”? CLATEMAN: “White Flag” was kind of the one. That’s why we put it out as a single. MANOW: I don’t like “White Flag” that much. CLATEMAN: I like it. MANOW: I sound like a frog. MCGRAW: The crowd really liked it. I was surprised how much they liked it. MANOW: You were surprised? MCGRAW: Well… CLATEMAN: I love that song. How would you rate the album if you were at Pitchfork? What would you give it? MCGRAW: Even the best Pitchfork albums, they only ever give it like a 9.7, right? CLATEMAN: Yeah. MCGRAW: I really like “Happysad.” I really like “White Flag” and “Blueberries.” You start by liking one song, and then that song drags you into the rest of the album over time. I’ll probably listen to “White Flag” a bunch tomorrow, and then by this time next week, I’ll like another song on the album. CLATEMAN: Because then you get kind of hypnotized by the sound of that song and you’re like, “I want something similar.” MCGRAW: Isn’t there a song called “I Don’t Know”? CLATEMAN: Yeah. MCGRAW: That’s not my favorite now, but I can see it coming. In two weeks, that will be my favorite. CLATEMAN: I’m looking forward to liking this album. I think I’m going to. MANOW: Looking forward to liking it. CLATEMAN: We’re just being an open book because I feel like that’s what Bassvictim is about, trying to be really transparent. There’s probably other artists who would have made this album, and felt the way we feel about it, and they would just not release it. They would scrap it, and wait, and work on something else until they got it right. And I totally respect that way of working. MANOW: I actually don’t respect that at all. CLATEMAN: I respect it, but it’s not for me. MANOW: People who have that kind of perfectionism never end up releasing anything. If you’re afraid of making mistakes, it’s just an excuse. If you don’t like something and don’t release it, then how can you be sure that the next thing that you do is going to be amazing? It’s better to just release it and see what people think, because your art is not only for you. CLATEMAN: Me and Maria both enjoy relinquishing a degree of control over things. MANOW: Yeah. CLATEMAN: That’s why we work well together, because we enjoy randomness. We are in this process of letting go when we’re making the music. It almost feels like, once it’s made, it’s not even for us. I hardly ever revise and edit the music. Once the song’s completed, as in once Maria’s done all the vocal takes, there’s no version one, version two, or version three of any song. MANOW: Because that’s the biggest enemy of all artists and musicians. Perfectionism ends up killing so many talented people. We try to release as much as possible from the stuff that we’ve done. I’m also not going to be this kind of musician who knows that they don’t like their own album very much, but then they pretend to in every interview. We’re not going to fake our emotions, we’re not going to hide from them. CLATEMAN: If we never released the album, I would always hear it as this frustrated project that suffered and didn’t turn out how I imagined it would. But if we release it, I’m going to get to hear it totally differently. Once I see how people react to certain songs live, which songs become people’s favorites, I’m going to hear a new album. MANOW: If you can’t find the love for the album, at least find love for the stats that are going to come out. That’s my mentality. CLATEMAN: At least you can have love for the statistics. MANOW: I love seeing statistics from the albums, and just wondering why certain songs are favorites because, ultimately, you’re never going to know if it’s the production, or the lyrics—you’re never fully going to know what it is. CLATEMAN: Some songs become more popular later on. MANOW: It’s super interesting, seeing the growth. How in the first week, you would assume that the first song is going to have the most listens, but it’s not the case. And then seeing how sometimes songs get popular suddenly. “With You” was never a popular song, but all of a sudden it got quite popular. When we were doing a survey of our fans before our shows, a lot of people said “With You” was their favorite. And I had never even thought about that song, it was confusing. CLATEMAN: You just set the songs free. You open the gates, and let them out into the world to do their work. MANOW: Yeah. It’s so cool. MCGRAW: I remember after a show in L.A., there was this group of kids asking for photographs. But you were asking them, “What’s your favorite song? What’s your favorite song?” and they were all saying “Grow Up.” You asked why and they were like, “Oh, well, I’m growing up and it communicates that.” It was such a simple explanation. I feel like why I like a song is always some bullshit complex answer, but they were just like— CLATEMAN: “I’m growing up.” MCGR
